title: Database Design One to Many Relationships: 7 Steps to Create Them (With Examples)

best.what: the whole 7-step method (write a sentence, find the nouns, ask 'does A have many B', draw the tables, draw the line, add crow's foot) applies directly to designing Sheet tabs

why: Short, clear, repeatable method for spotting a one-to-many relationship before building any tables; the crow's foot notation is easier to grasp on screen than by ear.

title: How to Correctly Define Many-To-Many Relationships in Database Design

best.what: why you can't cram two class IDs in one cell, and the joining/junction table fix

why: The junction-table trick is exactly what a Sheet tab needs for things like 'students enrolled in many classes' - concrete, short, and correct.

title: SQL Joins: A Guide and Examples

best.what: what a join is and why you need one when data is split across tables

why: Pure SQL syntax (INNER/LEFT/RIGHT/FULL JOIN, ON clauses) - not something kids write in Sheets, but the teacher needs this to explain why 'lookup tables' work at all.

title: SQL Join 3 Tables: How-To with Example

best.what: chaining a second JOIN clause to bring in a third table

why: Straightforward SQL syntax extension; teacher reference only, no Sheets equivalent for kids to practice.

title: Self Join in SQL

best.what: the employee/manager and category/subcategory idea of a table pointing to itself

why: The SQL is teacher-only, but the underlying idea (a row referring to another row in the same tab, e.g. sub-categories) is a genuinely useful concept if a guide translates it to Sheets.

title: Database Design for Custom Fields

best.what: framing of the custom-fields problem (why 'let users add their own field' is hard to store)

why: Eight enterprise-grade solutions (EAV, JSON columns, dynamic schema) way beyond a 14-year-old's Sheets project; background reading for the teacher only.

title: Database Design: Product Attributes

best.what: product + size + color modeled with a joining table, short and clean

why: Good, tight example of a many-to-many joining table for product variants; solid extra example but not one of the top picks below.

title: Database Design for Chat Application

best.what: building message/contact/group tables from a plain-English feature list, then fixing a circular-relationship mistake live

why: A chat app is close to what these kids would actually vibe-code; shows requirements -> tables -> fix-your-mistake as a real process, not just a finished diagram.

title: 7 Database Design Mistakes to Avoid (With Solutions)

best.what: don't use a real-world value (SSN, part number) as your unique ID - use a made-up one
split optional fields like phone numbers into their own table instead of many empty columns

why: A good checklist of things that go wrong in first designs; some items (constraints, indexes) need a guide to translate into Sheets terms, but most transfer directly.

title: Database Design for Facebook: A Social Network Database Example

best.what: friendship as a many-to-many self-relationship, then posts/likes/comments

why: Clear and familiar app, but not one of the closest matches to what these kids will build; good extra example.

title: How I Designed the Hogwarts Database (Harry Potter Project)

best.what: students/houses/subjects/Quidditch teams built up one requirement at a time, playful and game-like

why: The closest thing in this group to a 'design a database for a game' example - fun, familiar IP, still teaches real relationship concepts (many-to-many teams, self-join categories).

title: How to Design a Database

best.what: the general 5-step process: write your idea, find the nouns, add attributes, add relationships, review - worked through a doctor-appointment example

why: This is the master template - the process every other 'database for X' video in this group actually follows. Teach this one first.

title: How to Design a Database for Instagram

best.what: followers as a many-to-many self-relationship, and filters/effects as many-to-many too

why: Clear, familiar app and a good extra example, but Instagram itself isn't a project shape most of these kids would build.

title: A Better Way to Store Address Data in a Database

best.what: why one big address field is bad and splitting into separate fields (street, city, postcode...) is better

why: Short, concrete rule that maps directly onto a Sheets column layout: don't cram several facts into one cell.

title: eCommerce Database Design: Diagram & Explanation

best.what: products, variations (size/color) and product items modeled with joining tables

why: Solid design but dense (14 requirements, payment methods, promotions) with business/legal asides (storing card data); better as teacher reference than a kid's first watch.

title: Database Design for a Food Delivery App (Example & Walkthrough)

best.what: customer/restaurant/menu/order/driver tables built from 8 plain requirements, one at a time

why: Exactly the shape of app a group of these kids might pitch; requirements-to-tables walkthrough is clean and not too long.

title: The Best Way to Store Phone Numbers in an SQL Database

best.what: storing a phone number as a number silently drops the leading zero - store it as text instead

why: Short, very concrete gotcha that also bites kids in Google Sheets (number-formatted cells drop leading zeros too) - directly useful, not just SQL trivia.

title: Database Design: StackOverflow (Q&A Site)

best.what: tags (many-to-many), comments needing one link not two, and votes

why: Clean, teen-followable example and a nice case study in catching your own design mistake mid-video, but not one of the closest-fit picks.

title: Database Design for School Students for an Entire School

best.what: students, guardians, year levels and classes built from a 16-requirement list, many-to-many tables explained as they appear

why: A school system is a natural student-project idea and the most requirement-heavy, realistic walkthrough in the group - long, but sampleable in sections.

title: Database Design: Trello (Kanban Board App)

best.what: boards, lists, cards, board members and card members, all built feature-by-feature from screenshots of the real app

why: Directly matches a turn-based/task-tracker style app these kids could vibe-code; walks through the exact kind of design-from-a-real-app process we want them to learn.

title: Database Design for Real Estate Company

best.what: splitting a 'property' table into property + listing when the same property can be listed multiple times

why: Well-reasoned design (11 requirements) but built around business concepts (contracts, offers, agents) far from a teen project; teacher reference.

title: Database Design for a Train Booking System

best.what: journeys, stations and stop order via a many-to-many joining table

why: Solid and correct but fairly niche/complex (carriage classes, weekday vs weekend pricing) for a 14-year-old's first database project.

title: Database Design - similar records, what to do?

best.what: one shared 'person' table with a type column vs. separate tables per role, pros and cons of each

why: A genuinely useful design decision (e.g. 'one Users tab with a role column' vs 'a tab per role') that a guide could pose to kids directly, but the trade-off discussion is abstract for a first watch.

title: Database Design for a Hotel Management System

best.what: room classes, features and bed types linked through many-to-many joining tables

why: Thorough (12 requirements) but built around hotel-operations concepts less familiar to a teen than a chat app or Trello board.

title: eCommerce Product Database Design: Step-By-Step

best.what: modeling flexible filter attributes (EAV-style) with real CREATE/INSERT/ALTER SQL against a live ASOS-style store

why: 30+ minutes of live MySQL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, error-fixing) - a great advanced case study for the teacher, but far past raw SQL work these kids will do in Sheets.

title: Database Design for an Online Course Website

best.what: modules -> lessons -> quizzes -> questions -> answers, plus tracking student progress and quiz attempts

why: Relatable (a course/quiz platform) and clean, but not one of the closest-match picks; good extra example if a group builds a learning app.

title: How to Design a Database for AirBNB

best.what: properties, locations/countries as lookup tables, images, and favorites as a many-to-many

why: Long (18.8 min) and thorough, walking a real live website feature-by-feature, but the booking/host/review complexity is more than a first teen project needs.

title: I Critique a Database Design: My Honest Review

best.what: why char vs varchar matters and why a business-meaningful code shouldn't be the primary key

why: A great model of 'how an expert reviews someone else's design out loud' - useful for the teacher's own review process, but assumes SQL data-type knowledge kids won't have.
